verses.zh: 那两个天使晚上到了所多玛；罗得正坐在所多玛城门口，看见他们，就起来迎接，脸伏于地下拜，
verses.en: The two angels came to Sodom in the evening while[NOTE:1] Lot was sitting in the city’s gateway.[NOTE:2] When Lot saw them, he got up to meet them and bowed down with his face toward the ground.
notes: The disjunctive clause is temporal here, indicating what Lot was doing at the time of their arrival.

The expression sitting in the city’s gateway may mean that Lot was exercising some type of judicial function (see the use of the idiom in 2 Sam 19:8; Jer 26:10; 38:7; 39:3).tn Heb “sitting in the gate of Sodom.” The phrase “the gate of Sodom” has been translated “the city’s gateway” for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 说：「我主啊，请你们到仆人家里洗洗脚，住一夜，清早起来再走。」他们说：「不！我们要在街上过夜。」
verses.en: He said, “Here, my lords, please turn aside to your servant’s house. Stay the night[NOTE:1] and wash your feet. Then you can be on your way early in the morning.”[NOTE:2] “No,” they replied, “we’ll spend the night in the town square.”[NOTE:3]
notes: The imperatives have the force of invitation.
These two verbs form a verbal hendiadys: “you can rise up early and go” means “you can go early.”
The town square refers to the wide street area at the gate complex of the city.

verses.zh: 罗得切切地请他们，他们这才进去，到他屋里。罗得为他们预备筵席，烤无酵饼，他们就吃了。
verses.en: But he urged[NOTE:1] them persistently, so they turned aside with him and entered his house. He prepared a feast for them, including bread baked without yeast, and they ate.
notes: The Hebrew verb פָּצַר (patsar, “to press, to insist”) ironically foreshadows the hostile actions of the men of the city (see v. 9, where the verb also appears). The repetition of the word serves to contrast Lot to his world.

verses.zh: 他们还没有躺下，所多玛城里各处的人，连老带少，都来围住那房子，
verses.en: Before they could lie down to sleep,[NOTE:1] all the men—both young and old, from every part of the city of Sodom—surrounded the house.[NOTE:2]
notes: The verb שָׁכַב (shakhav) means “to lie down, to recline,” that is, “to go to bed.” Here what appears to be an imperfect is a preterite after the adverb טֶרֶם (terem). The nuance of potential (perfect) fits well.

Heb “and the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from the young to the old, all the people from the end [of the city].” The repetition of the phrase “men of” stresses all kinds of men.

verses.zh: 呼叫罗得说：「今日晚上到你这里来的人在哪里呢？把他们带出来，任我们所为。」
verses.en: They shouted to Lot,[NOTE:1] “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us so we can take carnal knowledge of[NOTE:2] them!”
notes: The Hebrew text adds “and said to him.” This is redundant in English and has not been translated for stylistic reasons.

The sin of the men of Sodom is debated. The fact that the sin involved a sexual act (see note on the phrase “take carnal knowledge of” in 19:5) precludes an association of the sin with inhospitality as is sometimes asserted (see W. Roth, “What of Sodom and Gomorrah? Homosexual Acts in the Old Testament,” Explor 1 [1974]: 7-14). The text at a minimum condemns forced sexual intercourse, i.e., rape. Other considerations, though, point to a condemnation of homosexual acts more generally. The narrator emphasizes the fact that the men of Sodom wanted to have sex with men: They demand that Lot release the angelic messengers (seen as men) to them for sex, and when Lot offers his daughters as a substitute they refuse them and attempt to take the angelic messengers by force. In addition the wider context of the Pentateuch condemns homosexual acts as sin (see, e.g., Lev 18:22). Thus a reading of this text within its narrative context, both immediate and broad, condemns not only the attempted rape but also the attempted homosexual act.tn Heb “know.” The expression יָדַע (yadaʿ) “to know” is a euphemism for sexual relations. Elsewhere NET employs the English euphemism “be intimate with” for this use of יָדַע, but uses a different euphemism here because of the perverse overtones of force in this context. Their intent is to molest them, but their rhetoric tries to minimize their wickedness.

verses.zh: 罗得出来，把门关上，到众人那里，
verses.en: Lot went outside to them, shutting the door behind him.

verses.zh: 说：「众弟兄，请你们不要做这恶事。
verses.en: He said, “No, my brothers! Don’t act so wickedly![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “may my brothers not act wickedly.”

verses.zh: 我有两个女儿，还是处女，容我领出来，任凭你们的心愿而行；只是这两个人既然到我舍下，不要向他们做甚么。」
verses.en: Look, I have two daughters who have never been intimate with[NOTE:1] a man. Let me bring them out to you, and you can do to them whatever you please.[NOTE:2] Only don’t do anything to these men, for they have come under the protection[NOTE:3] of my roof.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “who have not known.” Here this expression is a euphemism for sexual relations.
Heb “according to what is good in your eyes.”
Heb “shadow.”

This chapter portrays Lot as a hypocrite. He is well aware of the way the men live in his city and is apparently comfortable in the midst of it. But when confronted by the angels, he finally draws the line. But he is nevertheless willing to sacrifice his daughters’ virginity to protect his guests. His opposition to the crowds leads to his rejection as a foreigner by those with whom he had chosen to live. The one who attempted to rescue his visitors ends up having to be rescued by them.

verses.zh: 众人说：「退去吧！」又说：「这个人来寄居，还想要作官哪！现在我们要害你比害他们更甚。」众人就向前拥挤罗得，要攻破房门。
verses.en: “Out of our way!”[NOTE:1] they cried, “This man came to live here as a foreigner,[NOTE:2] and now he dares to judge us![NOTE:3] We’ll do more harm[NOTE:4] to you than to them!” They kept pressing in on Lot[NOTE:5] until they were close enough[NOTE:6] to break down the door.
notes: Heb “approach out there” which could be rendered “Get out of the way, stand back!”
Heb “to live as a resident foreigner.”
Heb “and he has judged, judging.” The infinitive absolute follows the finite verbal form for emphasis. This emphasis is reflected in the translation by the phrase “dares to judge.”

The verb “to do wickedly” is repeated here (see v. 7). It appears that whatever “wickedness” the men of Sodom had intended to do to Lot’s visitors—probably nothing short of homosexual rape—they were now ready to inflict on Lot.
Heb “and they pressed against the man, against Lot, exceedingly.”
Heb “and they drew near.”

verses.zh: 只是那二人伸出手来，将罗得拉进屋去，把门关上，
verses.en: So the men inside[NOTE:1] reached out[NOTE:2] and pulled Lot back into the house[NOTE:3] as they shut the door.
notes: Heb “the men,” referring to the angels inside Lot’s house. The word “inside” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
The Hebrew text adds “their hand.” These words have not been translated for stylistic reasons.
Heb “to them into the house.”

verses.zh: 并且使门外的人，无论老少，眼都昏迷；他们摸来摸去，总寻不着房门。
verses.en: Then they struck the men who were at the door of the house, from the youngest to the oldest,[NOTE:1] with blindness. The men outside[NOTE:2] wore themselves out trying to find the door.
notes: Heb “from the least to the greatest.”
Heb “they”; the referent (the men of Sodom outside the door) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 二人对罗得说：「你这里还有甚么人吗？无论是女婿是儿女，和这城中一切属你的人，你都要将他们从这地方带出去。
verses.en: Then the two visitors[NOTE:1] said to Lot, “Who else do you have here?[NOTE:2] Do you have[NOTE:3] any sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or other relatives in the city?[NOTE:4] Get them out of this[NOTE:5] place
notes: Heb “the men,” referring to the angels inside Lot’s house. The word “visitors” has been supplied in the translation for clarity.
Heb “Yet who [is there] to you here?”
The words “Do you have” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.
Heb “a son-in-law and your sons and your daughters and anyone who (is) to you in the city.”
Heb “the place.” The Hebrew article serves here as a demonstrative.

verses.zh: 我们要毁灭这地方；因为城内罪恶的声音在耶和华面前甚大，耶和华差我们来，要毁灭这地方。」
verses.en: because we are about to destroy[NOTE:1] it. The outcry against this place[NOTE:2] is so great before the Lord that he[NOTE:3] has sent us to destroy it.”
notes: The Hebrew participle expresses an imminent action here.
Heb “for their outcry.” The words “this place” have been moved from earlier in the sentence for stylistic reasons, and "about" has been added.
Heb “the Lord.” The repetition of the divine name has been replaced in the translation by the pronoun “he” for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 罗得就出去，告诉娶了（或译：将要娶）他女儿的女婿们说：「你们起来离开这地方，因为耶和华要毁灭这城。」他女婿们却以为他说的是戏言。
verses.en: Then Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law who were going to marry his daughters.[NOTE:1] He said, “Quick, get out of this place because the Lord is about to destroy[NOTE:2] the city!” But his sons-in-law thought he was ridiculing them.[NOTE:3]
notes: The language has to be interpreted in the light of the context and the social customs. The men are called “sons-in-law” (literally “the takers of his daughters”), but the daughters had not yet had sex with a man. It is better to translate the phrase “who were going to marry his daughters.” Since formal marriage contracts were binding, the husbands-to-be could already be called sons-in-law.
The Hebrew active participle expresses an imminent action.

Heb “and he was like one taunting in the eyes of his sons-in-law.” These men mistakenly thought Lot was ridiculing them and their lifestyle. Their response illustrates how morally insensitive they had become.

verses.zh: 天明了，天使催逼罗得说：「起来！带着你的妻子和你在这里的两个女儿出去，免得你因这城里的罪恶同被剿灭。」
verses.en: At dawn[NOTE:1] the angels hurried Lot along, saying, “Get going! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here,[NOTE:2] or else you will be destroyed when the city is judged!”[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “When dawn came up.”
Heb “who are found.” The wording might imply he had other daughters living in the city, but the text does not explicitly state this.
Or “with the iniquity [i.e., punishment] of the city” (cf. NASB, NRSV).

verses.zh: 但罗得迟延不走。二人因为耶和华怜恤罗得，就拉着他的手和他妻子的手，并他两个女儿的手，把他们领出来，安置在城外；
verses.en: When Lot[NOTE:1] hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and two daughters because the Lord had compassion on them.[NOTE:2] They led them away and placed them[NOTE:3] outside the city.
notes: Heb “he”; the referent (Lot) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Heb “in the compassion of the Lord to them.”

Heb “brought him out and placed him.” The third masculine singular suffixes refer specifically to Lot, though his wife and daughters accompanied him (see v. 17). For stylistic reasons these have been translated as plural pronouns (“them”).

verses.zh: 领他们出来以后，就说：「逃命吧！不可回头看，也不可在平原站住。要往山上逃跑，免得你被剿灭。」
verses.en: When they had brought them outside, they[NOTE:1] said, “Run[NOTE:2] for your lives! Don’t look[NOTE:3] behind you or stop anywhere in the valley![NOTE:4] Escape to the mountains or you will be destroyed!”
notes: Or “one of them”; Heb “he.” Several ancient versions (LXX, Vulgate, Syriac) read the plural “they.” See also the note on “your” in v. 19.
Heb “escape.”
The Hebrew verb translated “look” signifies an intense gaze, not a passing glance. This same verb is used later in v. 26 to describe Lot’s wife’s self-destructive look back at the city.
Or “in the plain”; Heb “in the circle,” referring to the “circle” or oval area of the Jordan Valley.

verses.zh: 罗得对他们说：「我主啊，不要如此！
verses.en: But Lot said to them, “No, please, Lord![NOTE:1]
notes: Or “my lords.” See the following note on the problem of identifying the addressee here. The Hebrew term is אֲדֹנָי (ʾadonay).

verses.zh: 你仆人已经在你眼前蒙恩；你又向我显出莫大的慈爱，救我的性命。我不能逃到山上去，恐怕这灾祸临到我，我便死了。
verses.en: Your[NOTE:1] servant has found favor with you,[NOTE:2] and you have shown me great[NOTE:3] kindness[NOTE:4] by sparing[NOTE:5] my life. But I am not able to escape to the mountains because[NOTE:6] this disaster will overtake[NOTE:7] me and I’ll die.[NOTE:8]
notes: The second person pronominal suffixes are singular in this verse (note “your eyes,” “you have made great,” and “you have acted”). Verse 18a seems to indicate that Lot is addressing the angels, but the use of the singular and the appearance of the divine title “Lord” (אֲדֹנָי, ʾadonay) in v. 18b suggests he is speaking to God.
Heb “in your eyes.”
Heb “you made great your kindness.”
The Hebrew word חֶסֶד (khesed) can refer to “faithful love” or to “kindness,” depending on the context. The precise nuance here is uncertain. tn Heb “kindness that you have done with me.”
The infinitive construct explains how God has shown Lot kindness.
Heb “lest.”
The Hebrew verb דָּבַק (davaq) normally means “to stick to, to cleave, to join.” Lot is afraid he cannot outrun the coming calamity.
The perfect verb form with vav consecutive carries the nuance of the imperfect verbal form before it.

verses.zh: 看哪，这座城又小又近，容易逃到，这不是一个小的吗？求你容我逃到那里，我的性命就得存活。」
verses.en: Look, this town[NOTE:1] over here is close enough to escape to, and it’s just a little one.[NOTE:2] Let me go there.[NOTE:3] It’s just a little place, isn’t it?[NOTE:4] Then I’ll survive.”[NOTE:5]
notes: The Hebrew word עִיר (ʿir) can refer to either a city or a town, depending on the size of the place. Given that this place was described by Lot later in this verse as a “little place,” the translation uses “town.”
Heb “Look, this town is near to flee to there. And it is little.”
Heb “Let me escape to there.” The cohortative here expresses Lot’s request.
Heb “Is it not little?”
Heb “my soul will live.” After the cohortative the jussive with vav conjunctive here indicates purpose/result.

verses.zh: 天使对他说：「这事我也应允你；我不倾覆你所说的这城。
verses.en: “Very well,” he replied,[NOTE:1] “I will grant this request too[NOTE:2] and will not overthrow[NOTE:3] the town you mentioned.
notes: Heb “And he said to him, ‘Look, . . . .’” The order of the clauses has been rearranged for stylistic reasons. The referent of the speaker (“he”) is somewhat ambiguous: It could be taken as the angel to whom Lot has been speaking (so NLT; note the singular references in vv. 18-19), or it could be that Lot is speaking directly to the Lord here. Most English translations leave the referent of the pronoun unspecified and maintain the ambiguity.
Heb “I have lifted up your face [i.e., shown you favor] also concerning this matter.”

The negated infinitive construct indicates either the consequence of God’s granting the request (“I have granted this request, so that I will not”) or the manner in which he will grant it (“I have granted your request by not destroying”).

verses.zh: 你要速速地逃到那城；因为你还没有到那里，我不能做甚么。」因此那城名叫琐珥（就是小的意思）。
verses.en: Run there quickly,[NOTE:1] for I cannot do anything until you arrive there.” (This incident explains why the town was called Zoar.)[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “Be quick! Escape to there!” The two imperatives form a verbal hendiadys, the first becoming adverbial.

Heb “Therefore the name of the city is called Zoar.” The name of the place, צוֹעַר (tsoʿar) apparently means “Little Place,” in light of the wordplay with the term “little” (מִצְעָר, mitsʿar) used twice by Lot to describe the town (v. 20).

verses.zh: 罗得到了琐珥，日头已经出来了。
verses.en: The sun had just risen[NOTE:1] over the land as Lot reached Zoar.[NOTE:2]
notes: The sun had just risen. There was very little time for Lot to escape between dawn (v. 15) and sunrise (here).

The juxtaposition of the two disjunctive clauses indicates synchronic action. The first action (the sun’s rising) occurred as the second (Lot’s entering Zoar) took place. The disjunctive clauses also signal closure for the preceding scene.

verses.zh: 当时，耶和华将硫磺与火从天上耶和华那里降与所多玛和蛾摩拉，
verses.en: Then the Lord rained down[NOTE:1] sulfur and fire[NOTE:2] on Sodom and Gomorrah. It was sent down from the sky by the Lord.[NOTE:3]
notes: The disjunctive clause signals the beginning of the next scene and highlights God’s action.
Or “burning sulfur” (the traditional “fire and brimstone”).

Heb “from the Lord from the heavens.” The words “It was sent down” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.sn The text explicitly states that the sulfur and fire that fell on Sodom and Gomorrah was sent down from the sky by the Lord. What exactly this was, and how it happened, can only be left to intelligent speculation, but see J. P. Harland, “The Destruction of the Cities of the Plain,” BA 6 (1943): 41-54.

verses.zh: 把那些城和全平原，并城里所有的居民，连地上生长的，都毁灭了。
verses.en: So he overthrew those cities and all that region,[NOTE:1] including all the inhabitants of the cities and the vegetation that grew from the ground.[NOTE:2]
notes: Or “and all the plain”; Heb “and all the circle,” referring to the “circle” or oval area of the Jordan Valley.
Heb “and what sprouts of the ground.”

verses.zh: 罗得的妻子在后边回头一看，就变成了一根盐柱。
verses.en: But Lot’s[NOTE:1] wife looked back longingly[NOTE:2] and was turned into a pillar of salt.
notes: Heb “his”; the referent (Lot) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The Hebrew verb means “to look intently; to gaze” (see 15:5).sn Longingly. Lot’s wife apparently identified with the doomed city and thereby showed lack of respect for God’s provision of salvation. She, like her daughters later, had allowed her thinking to be influenced by the culture of Sodom.

verses.zh: 亚伯拉罕清早起来，到了他从前站在耶和华面前的地方，
verses.en: Abraham got up early in the morning and went[NOTE:1] to the place where he had stood before the Lord.
notes: The words “and went” are supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons.

verses.zh: 向所多玛和蛾摩拉与平原的全地观看，不料，那地方烟气上腾，如同烧窑一般。
verses.en: He looked out toward[NOTE:1] Sodom and Gomorrah and all the land of that region.[NOTE:2] As he did so, he saw the smoke rising up from the land like smoke from a furnace.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “upon the face of.”
Or “all the land of the plain”; Heb “and all the face of the land of the circle,” referring to the “circle” or oval area of the Jordan Valley.

Heb “And he saw, and look, the smoke of the land went up like the smoke of a furnace.”sn It is hard to imagine what was going on in Abraham’s mind, but this brief section in the narrative enables the reader to think about the human response to the judgment. Abraham had family in that area. He had rescued those people from the invasion. That was why he interceded. Yet he surely knew how wicked they were. That was why he got the number down to ten when he negotiated with God to save the city. But now he must have wondered, “What was the point?”

verses.zh: 当　神毁灭平原诸城的时候，他记念亚伯拉罕，正在倾覆罗得所住之城的时候，就打发罗得从倾覆之中出来。
verses.en: So when God destroyed[NOTE:1] the cities of the region,[NOTE:2] God honored[NOTE:3] Abraham’s request. He removed Lot[NOTE:4] from the midst of the destruction when he destroyed[NOTE:5] the cities Lot had lived in.
notes: The construction is a temporal clause comprised of the temporal indicator, an infinitive construct with a preposition, and the subjective genitive.
Or “of the plain”; Heb “of the circle,” referring to the “circle” or oval area of the Jordan Valley.

God showed Abraham special consideration because of the covenantal relationship he had established with the patriarch. Yet the reader knows that God delivered the “righteous” (Lot’s designation in 2 Pet 2:7) before destroying their world—which is what he will do again at the end of the age.tn Heb “remembered,” but this means more than mental recollection here. Abraham’s request (Gen 18:23-32) was that the Lord not destroy the righteous with the wicked. While the requisite minimum number of righteous people (ten, v. 32) needed for God to spare the cities was not found, God nevertheless rescued the righteous before destroying the wicked.
God’s removal of Lot before the judgment is paradigmatic. He typically delivers the godly before destroying their world.
Heb “the overthrow when [he] overthrew.”

verses.zh: 罗得因为怕住在琐珥，就同他两个女儿从琐珥上去，住在山里；他和两个女儿住在一个洞里。
verses.en: Lot went up from Zoar with his two daughters and settled in the mountains because he was afraid to live in Zoar. So he lived in a cave with his two daughters.

verses.zh: 大女儿对小女儿说：「我们的父亲老了，地上又无人按着世上的常规进到我们这里。
verses.en: Later the older daughter said[NOTE:1] to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the country[NOTE:2] to sleep with us,[NOTE:3] the way everyone does.
notes: Heb “and the firstborn said.”

Or perhaps “on earth,” in which case the statement would be hyperbolic. sn Presumably there had been some men living in the town of Zoar to which Lot and his daughters had initially fled. Perhaps they feared that the destruction was more widespread than it really was, or perhaps they feared some sort of stigma following the disaster that fell on their former town.

Heb “to come over us according to the manner of the whole world.” “To come over us” is a euphemism for sexual relations. “According to the manner of the whole world” is an idiom for what is customary and normal, elsewhere (Josh 23:14; 1 Kgs 2:2) used to describe dying.

verses.zh: 来！我们可以叫父亲喝酒，与他同寝。这样，我们好从他存留后裔。」
verses.en: Come, let’s make our father drunk with wine[NOTE:1] so we can go to bed with[NOTE:2] him and preserve[NOTE:3] our family line through our father.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “drink wine.”

Heb “and we will lie down with.” The cohortative with vav (ו) conjunctive is subordinated to the preceding cohortative and indicates purpose or result. The phrase “to lie down with” is a euphemism for sexual relations; the translation, in turn, also supplies a euphemism.
Or “that we may preserve.” Here the cohortative with vav (ו) conjunctive indicates their ultimate goal.

Heb “and we will keep alive from our father descendants.”sn For a discussion of the cultural background of the daughters’ desire to preserve our family line see F. C. Fensham, “The Obliteration of the Family as Motif in the Near Eastern Literature,” AION 10 (1969): 191-99.

verses.zh: 于是，那夜她们叫父亲喝酒，大女儿就进去和她父亲同寝；她几时躺下，几时起来，父亲都不知道。
verses.en: So that night they made their father drunk with wine,[NOTE:1] and the older daughter[NOTE:2] came in and went to bed with[NOTE:3] her father. But he was not aware of when she lay down with him or when she got up.
notes: Heb “drink wine.”
Heb “the firstborn.”
Heb “came and lied down with.” Both of the expressions can be a euphemism for sexual relations. See the note at 2 Sam 12:24.

verses.zh: 第二天，大女儿对小女儿说：「我昨夜与父亲同寝。今夜我们再叫他喝酒，你可以进去与他同寝。这样，我们好从父亲存留后裔。」
verses.en: So in the morning the older daughter[NOTE:1] said to the younger, “Since I went to bed with[NOTE:2] my father last night, let’s make him drunk[NOTE:3] again tonight. Then you go in and go to bed with him so we can preserve our family line through our father.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “the firstborn.”
Heb “to lie with.” The phrase is a euphemism for sexual relations.
Heb “Let’s make him drink wine.”
Heb “And we will keep alive descendants from our father.”

verses.zh: 于是，那夜她们又叫父亲喝酒，小女儿起来与她父亲同寝；她几时躺下，几时起来，父亲都不知道。
verses.en: So they made their father drunk[NOTE:1] that night as well, and the younger one came and went to bed with him.[NOTE:2] But he was not aware of when she lay down with him or when she got up.
notes: Heb “drink wine.”
Heb “lied down with him.”

verses.zh: 这样，罗得的两个女儿都从她父亲怀了孕。
verses.en: In this way both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their father.

verses.zh: 大女儿生了儿子，给他起名叫摩押，就是现今摩押人的始祖。
verses.en: The older daughter[NOTE:1] gave birth to a son and named him Moab.[NOTE:2] He is the ancestor of the Moabites of today.
notes: Heb “the firstborn.”

The meaning of the name Moab is not certain. The name sounds like the Hebrew phrase “from our father” (מֵאָבִינוּ, meʾavinu) which the daughters used twice (vv. 32, 34). This account is probably included in the narrative in order to portray the Moabites, who later became enemies of God’s people, in a negative light.

verses.zh: 小女儿也生了儿子，给他起名叫便・亚米，就是现今亚扪人的始祖。
verses.en: The younger daughter also gave birth to a son and named him Ben Ammi.[NOTE:1] He is the ancestor of the Ammonites of today.
notes: The name Ben Ammi means “son of my people.” Like the account of Moab’s birth, this story is probably included in the narrative to portray the Ammonites, another perennial enemy of Israel, in a negative light.
